lessons.title: Environmental, Ethical and Legal Issues
lessons.description: Energy costs, e-waste, data privacy, and UK laws protecting personal data and creative work.
lessons.content_html:
Why Technology Has Consequences

Every device you use, every app you run, and every file you upload has costs and consequences beyond its obvious function. These fall into three categories: environmental issues, ethical issues, and legal issues. Understanding all three helps you evaluate technology honestly — not just what it can do, but what it costs and what rules govern its use.

Environmental Impact: Manufacture

A digital device does not start its environmental life when you switch it on — it starts when its materials are extracted from the ground. Producing a smartphone, laptop or server requires mining rare earth minerals and metals such as lithium, cobalt, copper and gold. These mining operations can cause habitat destruction, water pollution and significant carbon emissions. The energy-intensive fabrication processes used to manufacture processors and circuit boards add further to the carbon cost. Every new device purchased represents environmental impact before the device is even used.

Environmental Impact: Energy Consumption in Use

Running digital devices and the infrastructure that supports them requires vast amounts of electricity. Data centres power the internet, cloud services and streaming platforms. They run continuously and require cooling systems — which themselves consume electricity and water — to prevent equipment from overheating. Individual devices (phones, laptops, televisions) consume energy throughout their lifetimes, and wireless network infrastructure (mobile masts, routers) requires continuous power to operate.

Key Fact

The four stages of a device’s environmental impact are: manufacture (mining, fabrication emissions), energy consumption in use (data centres, devices, networks), replacement cycle (how often devices are upgraded), and disposal (e-waste and toxic materials).

Environmental Impact: Replacement Cycle and Disposal

The rate at which consumers replace devices matters. When manufacturers design products to become outdated or to stop receiving software updates after a few years — a practice sometimes called planned obsolescence — they accelerate the replacement cycle. Each discarded device becomes e-waste (electronic waste). Devices contain hazardous substances including lead, mercury and cadmium. When sent to landfill, these substances can leach into soil and groundwater. Informal recycling in some regions exposes workers to toxic chemicals. Responsible disposal requires using official recycling or manufacturer take-back schemes.

Individuals can help by repairing rather than replacing devices, choosing refurbished hardware, and using official recycling and take-back schemes. Manufacturers can design products that are easier to repair, use more recycled materials, and provide software support for longer. Organisations can choose data centre providers that run on renewable energy or use waste-heat recovery. Technology can also reduce other environmental harms: remote working cuts commuting emissions, digital documents replace paper, and smart energy systems can optimise heating and lighting in buildings.

Ethical Issues: Privacy and Personal Data

Privacy is the central ethical concern of the digital age. Every time you use a smartphone, banking app or social media platform, data about you is collected — your location, browsing history, financial transactions and social connections. Most people value the ability to control what others know about them. Privacy is challenged when organisations collect data that goes beyond what is necessary, share it without consent, or use it in ways users did not expect.

Three key ethical questions arise around personal data:

  • Ownership — who owns the data generated by your activity online? In many cases, the platform that collects it claims ownership, even when it relates entirely to your behaviour and preferences.
  • Consent — have users genuinely agreed to their data being collected and used in specific ways? Long, complex privacy policies can obscure the scope of what users are agreeing to.
  • Misuse — data collected for one purpose (for example, measuring fitness activity) could be shared with insurers or employers and used to make decisions that affect a person’s life without their knowledge.
Key Fact

Three ethical dimensions of personal data: ownership (who holds rights over data you generate?), consent (have users genuinely agreed to how data is used?), misuse (can data collected for one purpose be used in ways that harm the person?). All three are addressed by the Data Protection Act 2018.

UK Data Protection Law

The Data Protection Act 2018 governs how organisations handle personal data. It incorporates the requirements of UK GDPR (the UK’s retained version of European data protection regulation). Under the Act, organisations must: collect data only for a specific, stated purpose; keep it secure; not hold it for longer than necessary; and give individuals the right to access, correct or request deletion of their own data. Failure to comply can result in significant fines from the Information Commissioner’s Office. The Act replaced the earlier Data Protection Act 1998.

Intellectual Property: Copyright, Patents, Trademarks and Licencing

When someone creates software, music, a logo or an invention, they have rights over that creation. Intellectual property law protects those rights. There are four types you need to know.

Copyright — protected in the UK by the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988. Creative works — including software, music, images, films and written content — are automatically protected from the moment of creation. Copying or distributing copyrighted material without permission is illegal, even for personal rather than commercial use.

Patents — a patent gives an inventor the exclusive right to make, use or sell an invention for a limited period (typically 20 years in the UK). In return, the inventor publishes how the invention works. Patents can protect hardware designs and algorithms in some circumstances, but pure software ideas are generally not patentable in the UK.

Trademarks — a trademark protects a distinctive name, logo or symbol associated with a product or brand. Technology companies register trademarks to prevent competitors from using confusingly similar names or logos. Unlike copyright, trademarks must be formally registered and renewed to maintain protection.

Licencing — a software licence is a legal agreement between the rights holder and a user, setting out what the user may do with the software. A proprietary licence restricts copying, modification and redistribution. An open-source licence (such as the GNU GPL) permits users to view, modify and share the source code, subject to conditions. Using software outside the terms of its licence is a breach of copyright law.

The Computer Misuse Act 1990

The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes it a criminal offence to access a computer system without authorisation. It covers three categories of offence: gaining unauthorised access to computer material (for example, logging into someone else’s account without their permission); gaining unauthorised access with intent to commit or facilitate a further offence (for example, accessing a network to commit fraud); and making unauthorised modifications to computer material (for example, installing malware or deleting data). A 2015 amendment to the Act increased maximum penalties and extended its coverage to attacks on computer infrastructure. Hackers can face imprisonment and unlimited fines under this legislation.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For Explain questions on legal issues, always state the law’s name and year, then explain what it prohibits or requires — a bare name earns no marks. For Discuss questions on environmental impact, structure your answer around the four stages (manufacture, energy use, replacement cycle, disposal) and include at least one way to reduce each impact. For questions on intellectual property, be precise: copyright protects creative works automatically; patents must be applied for; trademarks must be registered; licences are contractual agreements, not a form of IP protection in themselves.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Digital devices have environmental costs across four stages: manufacture (mining and fabrication), energy use in operation (data centres, devices, networks), replacement cycle (planned obsolescence), and disposal (e-waste with toxic materials).
  • Personal data raises ethical issues of ownership, consent and misuse; the Data Protection Act 2018 gives individuals rights over their data and imposes obligations on organisations. The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes hacking criminal.
  • Intellectual property is protected in four ways: copyright (automatic, protects creative works including software), patents (registered, time-limited, protects inventions), trademarks (registered, protects brand identity), and licences (contractual terms for permitted use).

practice_questions.text: State the name and year of the UK law that gives individuals the right to request deletion of their personal data held by an organisation.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering/Secure: Data Protection Act 2018. Developing: Data Protection Act (year missing or wrong). Emerging: Any other act named.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'planned obsolescence' and explain one environmental consequence it causes.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Planned obsolescence is the practice of designing products to become outdated or to lose software support after a limited period (1), encouraging consumers to replace devices sooner than necessary (1); this increases the volume of e-waste generated (1); discarded devices contain hazardous materials such as lead and mercury that can leach into soil and groundwater if sent to landfill (1). Secure: Correct definition plus one environmental consequence clearly explained. Developing: Planned obsolescence described but consequence vague or not linked to specific harm. Emerging: Term used without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ethical concerns raised by organisations collecting personal data from users.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Ownership — the platform that collects data may claim ownership even though the data relates to the user's personal behaviour; this raises the question of who has rightful control (1+1). Consent — users may not have meaningfully agreed to their data being used in specific ways; long, complex privacy policies can obscure what is actually being consented to (1+1). Misuse — data collected for one purpose (e.g. fitness tracking) could be shared with insurers or employers and used to make decisions that negatively affect the user (1+1). Award any two concerns fully explained. Secure: Two clear concerns with explanation. Developing: One clear concern explained; second is vague. Emerging: Privacy mentioned without explanation.

practice_questions.text: A software developer writes a new application. Identify the type of intellectual property protection that automatically applies to this software from the moment it is created.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering/Secure: Copyright. Developing: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act (acceptable — identifies the correct law). Emerging: Patent or trademark (incorrect — these require registration).

Mastering: A legal agreement between the rights holder and a user that sets out the terms under which software may be used, modified or distributed (2). Secure: Mentions legal agreement and permitted use (2). Developing: Partial — describes a licence as 'permission to use software' without mentioning legal/contractual nature (1). Emerging: Vague description with no legal dimension (0).

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that the benefits of collecting large amounts of personal data outweigh the ethical and legal risks involved.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Benefits — personalised services improve user experience; health monitoring data can improve medical outcomes; analytics can drive business efficiency and economic growth (two developed points). Risks — privacy breaches expose sensitive data; misuse of data by insurers or employers can cause real harm; individuals often lack meaningful consent; organisations may prioritise profit over user welfare; legal obligations (Data Protection Act 2018) can be difficult to enforce globally (two developed points). Evaluation — weighs both sides; reaches a justified position acknowledging trade-offs between social benefit and individual rights. Secure: Both sides addressed with development; evaluation present. Developing: One side well-developed; other side listed without development; evaluation absent or weak. Emerging: One-sided argument with little supporting reasoning.

lessons.title: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning and Robotics
lessons.description: Accountability, safety, algorithmic bias and legal liability: the ethics of AI and robotics.
lessons.content_html:
What Are AI, Machine Learning and Robotics?

Artificial intelligence (AI) refers to computer systems that perform tasks requiring human-like reasoning. Machine learning is a way of building AI: instead of programming a system with explicit rules, you feed it large amounts of training data and it learns to identify patterns. Robotics combines mechanical engineering with computing to create machines that act in the physical world — everything from factory assembly arms to autonomous vehicles. These three technologies are increasingly intertwined: modern robots use AI and machine learning to make decisions in real time.

The benefits of these technologies are considerable. AI systems can diagnose diseases from scan images with accuracy comparable to specialists. Machine learning can detect fraud in banking transactions in milliseconds. Robots can carry out dangerous or repetitive tasks that would harm or exhaust human workers. However, the same capabilities raise four distinct ethical issues that your exam focuses on: accountability, safety, algorithmic bias, and legal liability.

Key Fact

There are four named ethical issues for AI, machine learning and robotics: accountability (who is responsible for decisions made by AI?), safety (can AI systems fail in ways that harm people?), algorithmic bias (can AI systems discriminate unfairly?), and legal liability (who is legally at fault when AI causes harm?).

Issue 1: Accountability

Accountability in AI refers to the question of who is answerable when an AI system makes a decision that affects someone’s life. When a doctor makes a clinical decision, that doctor can be asked to explain their reasoning and held to professional standards. When an AI system makes the same decision, the reasoning may be opaque — even to the developers who built it. This opacity is sometimes called the “black box” problem: the system produces outputs without making the reasoning visible or auditable.

Consider an AI system used to decide whether to grant a loan application or whether a prisoner should be considered for early release. If the system rejects an application, the affected person may have no way to find out why, no clear process for challenging the decision, and no human decision-maker to appeal to. This raises serious concerns about fairness, transparency, and the ability of individuals to contest decisions that affect them.

Many powerful machine learning models — particularly deep learning systems trained on millions of data points — make predictions through thousands of weighted calculations that cannot be easily summarised in human-readable rules. Developers can test inputs and observe outputs but may not be able to explain why a specific prediction was made for a specific individual. This creates accountability gaps: if a patient is denied treatment or a job candidate is rejected, there may be no clear human accountable for that outcome and no mechanism to review whether the decision was fair.

Issue 2: Safety

Safety concerns arise when AI systems operate in high-stakes environments where failure has physical consequences. A machine learning model trained in the lab may encounter real-world situations that differ from its training data and behave unexpectedly. In medical diagnosis, a misclassification could lead to incorrect treatment. In an autonomous vehicle, an unexpected failure could cause a road collision. In industrial robotics, a malfunctioning arm could injure a worker.

Safety concerns are also raised by adversarial attacks: techniques that deliberately feed AI systems misleading input to cause errors. For example, small, imperceptible changes to an image can cause a well-trained image classifier to confidently produce a completely wrong output. If such vulnerabilities exist in safety-critical systems — such as those used for border control, medical imaging or autonomous navigation — the consequences could be serious.

Issue 3: Algorithmic Bias

Algorithmic bias occurs when a machine learning system produces outcomes that are systematically unfair to particular groups of people. This usually happens because the training data reflects historical patterns of human prejudice. If a hiring algorithm is trained on historical employment decisions made in an era of gender or racial discrimination, it may learn to replicate those same patterns — flagging candidates from certain groups as less suitable, not because they are, but because the historical data it learned from was biased.

Facial recognition technology provides another clear example. Studies have found that some commercially deployed facial recognition systems perform significantly less accurately on darker-skinned faces and on women, compared with lighter-skinned men. If such systems are used for identity verification or law enforcement purposes, they are more likely to produce errors that disadvantage the groups they perform worst on. The bias is not intentional — it emerges from training data that was not representative of the full population.

Key Fact

Algorithmic bias is caused by biased training data — if the historical data used to train an AI reflects past discrimination, the model learns to replicate it. Bias can also arise from unrepresentative data — if certain groups are underrepresented in training data, the model performs less accurately for those groups. Neither form of bias requires any intent to discriminate.

Issue 4: Legal Liability

Legal liability is the question of who bears legal responsibility when an AI system causes harm. Existing legal frameworks generally assume a human decision-maker: if a car crashes due to driver negligence, the driver is liable; if a product is defective, the manufacturer is liable. When an autonomous vehicle causes a collision while operating without a human driver, or when an AI system misdiagnoses a patient, the existing framework struggles to assign responsibility cleanly.

Potential parties include: the company that developed the AI software, the organisation that deployed the system, the engineer who designed the training process, or the dataset provider. In practice, contracts and insurance arrangements may allocate liability, but this creates inconsistency and leaves affected individuals uncertain about whether they can seek redress. Legislators and courts in the UK and internationally are actively working to develop legal frameworks that can address AI liability, but this remains an open and contested area.

An autonomous vehicle illustrates all four issues simultaneously. Accountability: if the car makes a decision in a near-miss scenario, who decided how that decision would be made, and can it be reviewed? Safety: what happens when the car encounters weather conditions, road layouts or unexpected obstacles not well-represented in its training data? Algorithmic bias: if pedestrian detection systems were trained predominantly on data from one type of setting, they may perform less reliably in other environments. Legal liability: if a collision occurs in fully autonomous mode, is the car manufacturer, the software developer or the vehicle owner responsible? The self-driving car is not the only AI system raising these questions — it is simply an unusually visible example of issues that apply across healthcare AI, predictive policing, recruitment software and financial systems.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For Discuss questions on AI ethics (6 marks), you must address more than one side — cover both benefits and risks, using the four named issues (accountability, safety, algorithmic bias, legal liability) as your framework. A common mistake is listing all four issues without developing any of them: pick two or three and explain the mechanism behind each, with a concrete example. For Explain questions (4 marks), every marking point needs a statement plus reasoning — don’t just say “AI can be biased”; explain what causes the bias and why it matters.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • AI, machine learning and robotics raise four distinct ethical issues: accountability (who is answerable for AI decisions?), safety (can AI fail in harmful ways?), algorithmic bias (can training data encode discrimination?), and legal liability (who is at fault when AI causes harm?).
  • Algorithmic bias is caused by biased or unrepresentative training data, not by intentional discrimination. The outcomes can still systematically disadvantage particular groups in high-stakes decisions such as hiring, lending or law enforcement.
  • Legal frameworks struggle to assign responsibility for AI-caused harm because they assume a human decision-maker. Determining whether the developer, deployer or dataset provider is liable remains an open legal question in the UK and internationally.

practice_questions.text: State one cause of algorithmic bias in a machine learning system.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering/Secure: Biased training data — the training data reflects historical human prejudice or discrimination (1). Also accept: unrepresentative training data — certain groups are underrepresented, causing the model to perform less accurately for those groups (1). Emerging: 'Bad data' without specifying bias or representation.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by 'accountability' as an ethical issue with artificial intelligence systems.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Accountability refers to the question of who is responsible for decisions made by an AI system (1); many AI systems are 'black boxes' whose reasoning cannot be explained (1); this means individuals cannot find out why a decision affecting them was made (1); and there is no clear human to hold responsible or appeal to (1). Secure: Correct definition with two explained consequences. Developing: Accountability defined vaguely or one point developed. Emerging: General statement about AI making decisions with no explanation of the accountability problem.

practice_questions.text: Explain why legal liability is a problem when an autonomous vehicle is involved in a collision.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Existing legal frameworks assume a human driver is responsible (1); when operating fully autonomously there is no human driver to hold liable (1); responsibility may fall on the vehicle manufacturer, software developer, deployment company or owner (1); it is unclear how to assign fault between these parties when an algorithm made the decision (1). Secure: Correct identification of the human-driver assumption and two possible liable parties. Developing: Notes liability is unclear but doesn't explain why existing frameworks fail. Emerging: States someone should be responsible but doesn't identify the structural problem.

practice_questions.text: Describe two safety risks associated with using AI systems in high-stakes environments.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Unexpected inputs — AI trained on specific data may encounter real-world situations outside its training distribution, leading to unreliable outputs (1+1 for description plus consequence). Adversarial attacks — deliberately crafted inputs can cause confident but entirely wrong outputs, posing risks in systems used for medical imaging or security (1+1 for description plus consequence). Secure: Two distinct risks described with a linked consequence for each. Developing: Two risks named without linking consequences. Emerging: One risk described.

practice_questions.text: A recruitment company uses a machine learning system to shortlist job applicants. Identify one ethical issue this raises and explain the potential harm caused.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Algorithmic bias (1); if the training data reflects historical hiring patterns where certain groups were discriminated against, the model may learn to replicate those patterns (1); this could result in candidates from those groups being systematically rejected not because of their suitability but because of the biases in the training data (1); this perpetuates inequality and causes real harm to individuals who deserve equal consideration (1). Also accept: accountability — if the system rejects a candidate, they may have no way to find out why or challenge the decision (1+1+1+1). Secure: Correct issue named plus mechanism of harm clearly explained. Developing: Issue named but mechanism described vaguely. Emerging: Issue named with no explanation of harm.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that the risks of using artificial intelligence in society outweigh the benefits.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Benefits — AI can diagnose diseases with specialist-level accuracy; machine learning detects financial fraud in milliseconds; robots remove workers from dangerous or repetitive tasks; autonomous systems can improve transport safety by removing human error (two developed points). Risks — algorithmic bias can perpetuate discrimination at scale; accountability gaps mean affected individuals cannot challenge decisions; legal liability frameworks are inadequate; safety failures in high-stakes systems can cause physical harm; displacement of jobs has social consequences (two developed points). Evaluation — weighs both sides; acknowledges that risk severity depends on the domain of deployment; reaches a justified position. Secure: Both sides addressed with development; evaluation present but brief. Developing: One side well-developed; other listed; evaluation absent. Emerging: One-sided answer with minimal development.

lessons.title: Cybersecurity: Threats and Protection
lessons.description: How malware and social engineering attack systems, and the five protections that defend them.
lessons.content_html:
Why Cybersecurity Matters

Cyber security is the field concerned with defending digital systems and data from attack. It affects everyone: a hospital storing patient records, a bank holding millions of account details, a school with pupil data, and an individual with a social media profile. Cyber threats do not require physical proximity — an attacker can target systems from anywhere in the world, which is what makes them so difficult to defend against.

Threats come from two broad directions. Some exploit technical weaknesses in software or networks. Others exploit the most unpredictable part of any system: the people using it. Understanding how attacks work is the first step towards building effective defences.

Malware: The Five Types

Malware (malicious software) is any program designed to cause harm. There are five types you need to know for your exam.

A computer virus attaches to an existing file or program. When the infected file is opened or shared — for example, via an email attachment or a USB drive — the virus copies itself to other files. Viruses require a host file and rely on user action to spread.

A worm is similar to a virus but does not need a host file. It spreads automatically across networks by exploiting security vulnerabilities, with no user action required. A single unpatched device on a network can allow a worm to propagate to every connected machine.

A trojan (or trojan horse) disguises itself as useful software — a free game, a codec update, a utility. Once installed, it operates silently, typically opening a back door that gives an attacker remote access. Unlike a virus or worm, a trojan does not self-replicate.

Ransomware encrypts the victim’s files, making them inaccessible, and then demands a ransom payment in exchange for the decryption key. High-profile ransomware attacks have targeted hospitals, councils and businesses. Even paying the ransom does not guarantee that files will be restored.

A key logger is a form of spyware that runs hidden in the background and records every key pressed on the device. Passwords, bank account details, messages and search terms are all captured. The collected data is transmitted back to the attacker without the user’s knowledge.

Key Fact

Five malware types: virus (attaches to files, needs user action to spread), worm (spreads automatically across networks, no host file needed), trojan (disguised as legitimate software, opens a back door), ransomware (encrypts files and demands payment), key logger (records keystrokes silently).

Technical Vulnerabilities

Hackers do not always need sophisticated malware — they can exploit weaknesses that organisations have failed to close. The two main technical vulnerabilities in this specification are unpatched software and out-of-date anti-malware.

When a software vulnerability is discovered, the developer releases a security patch — an update that closes the gap. Systems that have not applied the patch remain exposed. Attackers can find published details of known vulnerabilities and write code to exploit them. This is why applying software updates promptly matters: the update often closes a door that attackers are already trying to walk through. Similarly, anti-malware software that has not been updated cannot recognise the latest threats, leaving newer malware able to operate undetected.

Social Engineering

Social engineering targets human psychology rather than technical flaws. Attackers create believable scenarios or apply pressure to trick people into doing something that compromises security — revealing a password, clicking a link, or transferring money. Three forms appear in the specification.

Phishing arrives as an email or text message that appears to come from a trusted source — a bank, a delivery company, or a well-known service. It typically creates urgency (“Your account will be suspended unless you act now”) and directs the target to a fake website to harvest credentials. Spear phishing is a targeted variant aimed at a specific individual, using personalised details to make the deception more convincing.

Pretexting (sometimes called blagging) involves inventing a convincing story to gain access or information. An attacker might call a company helpdesk claiming to be an IT contractor who urgently needs a user’s credentials reset, or pose as a supplier requesting bank account details. The invented scenario creates a sense of authority or urgency that overrides the target’s normal caution.

Shouldering (shoulder surfing) is the simplest form of social engineering: physically watching someone enter private information. It can happen at cashpoints, on public transport, or in shared workspaces where someone observes a colleague typing a password or reading a confidential document.

The Five Protections

Defending digital systems requires a layered approach. Five specific protection methods are named in the specification: anti-malware software, encryption, acceptable use policies, backup, and recovery procedures. Together these form a defence strategy that addresses different points of failure.

Anti-malware software detects and removes malicious programs by comparing files and behaviour against databases of known threats and suspicious patterns. It works best when updated frequently so that definitions include the most recent threats. Anti-malware can catch known viruses, worms and trojans before they execute, and can quarantine suspicious files for review.

Encryption converts data into a scrambled form that can only be read by someone with the correct key. If an attacker intercepts encrypted data in transit or steals an encrypted file, they cannot read its contents without the key. Encryption protects data at rest (stored on a device or server) and in transit (moving across a network).

An acceptable use policy (AUP) sets out the rules governing how staff may use an organisation’s IT systems. It defines what is and is not permitted: which websites may be accessed, whether personal use is allowed, how sensitive data must be handled, and the penalties for misuse. A well-enforced AUP reduces the likelihood of employees accidentally (or deliberately) introducing threats through risky behaviour.

Backup involves regularly copying data to a separate location — an external drive, a secure server or a cloud service — so that if the original is lost, corrupted or encrypted by ransomware, the data can be restored. Backups must be frequent enough to limit data loss to an acceptable period and stored in a location not directly accessible from the primary system (to prevent ransomware encrypting the backup too).

Recovery procedures are the documented plans and steps an organisation follows after a successful attack or system failure. They specify who does what, in what order, to restore services and data. Without tested recovery procedures, even organisations with good backups may take much longer than necessary to return to normal operation after an incident.

Key Fact

The five named protections are: anti-malware software (detects and removes malicious programs), encryption (scrambles data so it is unreadable without a key), acceptable use policy (rules governing how staff use IT systems), backup (regularly copies data to a separate location), and recovery procedures (documented steps to restore systems after an attack).
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions on malware, be precise about what distinguishes each type: a virus needs a host file; a worm spreads automatically; a trojan disguises itself; ransomware encrypts files; a key logger records keystrokes. Mixing up these definitions costs marks. For questions on protections, the specification lists exactly five — anti-malware, encryption, acceptable use policies, backup and recovery procedures. Do not add others (firewalls, biometrics, two-factor authentication are not in this list). For Discuss questions, always cover both the threat landscape and the limitations of any protection — for example, anti-malware cannot detect threats it has not seen before.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Five malware types: viruses (spread via host files), worms (spread across networks automatically), trojans (disguised as legitimate software), ransomware (encrypts files for ransom), key loggers (record keystrokes silently).
  • Hackers also exploit technical vulnerabilities — unpatched software and out-of-date anti-malware — and use social engineering (phishing, pretexting, shouldering) to bypass technical defences by targeting people.
  • Five layered protections: anti-malware software, encryption, acceptable use policies, backup and recovery procedures. Together they address detection, data confidentiality, user behaviour, data recovery and incident response.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a worm?
A) Malware that attaches to a legitimate file and spreads when that file is opened
B) Malware that spreads automatically across networks without needing a host file
C) Malware disguised as useful software that opens a back door for an attacker
D) Malware that encrypts files and demands a ransom payment
practice_questions.marks: B) Malware that spreads automatically across networks without needing a host file [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the difference between a computer virus and a worm.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A virus attaches to a host file and requires user action (such as opening an infected attachment) to spread (1); a worm spreads automatically across networks by exploiting vulnerabilities, without needing a host file or user action (1). Secure: Key distinction (host file / automatic spread) clearly made. Developing: One feature of one type stated without comparison. Emerging: Both types mentioned with no meaningful distinction.

practice_questions.text: Explain what ransomware does and describe one measure an organisation could take to reduce the impact of a ransomware attack.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Ransomware encrypts the victim's files, making them inaccessible (1); it then demands a ransom payment, usually in cryptocurrency, in exchange for the decryption key (1). Measure: maintaining regular offline backups means that if files are encrypted by ransomware, they can be restored without paying the ransom (1); backups must be stored separately from the primary system to prevent the ransomware encrypting them too (1). Secure: Correct description of ransomware plus a valid, explained measure. Developing: Ransomware described; measure stated but not explained. Emerging: Ransomware described; measure absent or vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain what phishing is and describe one reason why it is effective at bypassing technical security measures.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Phishing uses fraudulent emails or messages that appear to come from a trusted source to trick users into revealing credentials or visiting a fake website (1+1); it is effective because it targets human psychology rather than technical flaws — no vulnerability in software needs to exist for phishing to succeed (1); a user who believes the message is genuine will voluntarily enter their credentials, bypassing password protection entirely (1). Secure: Correct definition and clear reason for effectiveness. Developing: Definition correct; effectiveness described vaguely as 'tricks people'. Emerging: Phishing described as 'fake emails' with no explanation of why it works.

Mastering: A formal written agreement that sets out the rules governing how employees or users may use an organisation's IT systems, networks and data, including what is permitted and the consequences of misuse (2). Secure: Mentions rules governing IT system use and consequences (2). Developing: Describes it as 'rules for using computers' without mentioning the formal/documented nature or consequences (1). Emerging: Vague description with no specific content (0).

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that technical protections such as anti-malware software and encryption are sufficient to protect an organisation's digital systems.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Arguments for sufficiency — anti-malware can detect and quarantine known threats before they execute; encryption makes intercepted data unreadable; together they address the two most common attack vectors (technical intrusion and data theft) (two developed points). Arguments against sufficiency — anti-malware cannot detect entirely new threats (zero-day attacks); encryption does not prevent social engineering where a user is tricked into voluntarily providing credentials; technical protections do not address unpatched software vulnerabilities; human behaviour is not governed by software; acceptable use policies and backup procedures are also necessary to address behaviour and recovery (two developed points). Evaluation — technical protections are necessary but not sufficient; a layered strategy including people, processes and technology is required. Secure: Both sides with development; evaluation present. Developing: One side well-developed; other side listed. Emerging: One-sided with minimal development.

glossary_terms.definition: The processes, practices and technologies designed to protect networks, computers, programs and data from attack, damage or unauthorised access.
An umbrella term for any software that is hostile, intrusive or designed to damage, disrupt or gain unauthorised access to a computer system.
A type of malware that attaches itself to legitimate files and spreads by copying itself when an infected file is opened or shared.
A type of malware that spreads automatically across networks without needing to attach to a file or require user action, exploiting security vulnerabilities to replicate itself.
Malware disguised as legitimate software that, once installed, opens a back door allowing an attacker to access the system remotely, without self-replicating.
Malware that encrypts a victim's files and demands a payment, typically in cryptocurrency, in exchange for the decryption key.
A type of spyware that secretly records every keystroke made on a device, capturing passwords, bank details and messages, and transmits the data to an attacker.
Software that has not had available security fixes applied, leaving known vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit.
Software that detects and removes malicious programs by comparing files and behaviour against a database of known threats and suspicious patterns.
The manipulation of people into giving up confidential information or taking actions that compromise security, by exploiting trust and psychological pressure rather than technical vulnerabilities.
A social engineering attack using fraudulent emails, text messages or fake websites to trick users into revealing passwords, bank details or other private information.
A social engineering technique in which an attacker creates a fabricated scenario to manipulate a target into revealing information or performing an action.
Observing a person's private information over their shoulder, for example watching someone enter a PIN at a cashpoint or reading a password as it is typed.
A formal written agreement that sets out the rules governing how employees or users may use an organisation's IT systems, networks and data, and the consequences of misuse.
